summary.text: Animal communication is the transfer of information from one or more non-human animals to others in a way that affects the receivers' current or future behavior.
When information from a sender changes a receiver's behavior it is called a signal, and it can be sent intentionally or unintentionally.
Animals pass on information through visual displays, facial gestures, colour change, sounds, echolocation and electrolocation.

items.prompt: A mouse picks up the scent of a cat that is trying to sneak up on it. How does animal communication treat this?

options.label: As communication only if the cat meant to send the scent
As communication, since information can be sent unintentionally
As something else, since a signal must be sent on purpose
As communication only if several receivers are present

items.explain: Information may be sent unintentionally, as when scent passes from predator to prey through kairomones.

items.prompt: Suppose a call always harmed those who heard it and acted on it, while helping only the animal calling. What does signalling theory predict?

options.label: It would spread, since only the sender needs to benefit
It would last only if the receivers could not hear it
It would be unlikely to last, since both sender and receiver should usually benefit
It would last if the call were also visual

items.explain: Signalling theory predicts that for a signal to be maintained in the population, both the sender and receiver should usually receive some benefit.

items.prompt: A herring gull chick pecks at the red spot on its parent's bill. What does the peck do?

options.label: It stimulates the parent to bring up food, completing the feeding signal
It warns the parent that a predator is near
It tells the parent the chick wants to leave the nest
It marks the chick as belonging to that parent

items.explain: The chick's tapping at the red spot stimulates the parent to regurgitate food and completes the feeding signal.

items.prompt: Scientists tested animals on following a gaze into the distance and on following a gaze around a barrier. What did the developmental evidence suggest?

options.label: Both kinds rely on exactly the same mental mechanism
Only the distant kind exists in any species
The barrier kind appears only in apes and dogs
The two kinds of gaze following probably rely on different cognitive mechanisms

items.explain: Developmental evidence indicates that simple and geometric gaze following probably rely on different cognitive mechanisms.

items.prompt: A male cuttlefish courts a female while rival males watch from his other side. What does he display?

options.label: A male pattern toward her and a female pattern toward the rivals
A female pattern toward her and a male pattern toward the rivals
A male pattern on both sides of his body
No pattern, because courtship signals are not used near rivals

items.explain: He shows a male pattern facing the female and a female pattern facing away, to deceive other males.

items.prompt: Researchers wanted to judge how much pain a mouse was feeling as it increased. What did Mogil use?

options.label: Changes in the colour of the mouse's skin
Changes in the squeaks the mouse made
Five recognizable facial expressions that appeared as pain grew
Changes in the speed the mouse ran

items.explain: Mogil studied mouse facial expressions at increasing pain and found five recognizable ones, including orbital tightening, nose and cheek bulge, and ear and whisker changes.
